nameStory: The Brown Prionid gets its name from its rich brown coloration and its membership in the prionid subfamily of longhorn beetles. 'Prionid' comes from the Greek word 'prion,' meaning saw, referring to the saw-toothed antennae that many species in this group possess.
description: The Brown Prionid is a large, robust longhorn beetle that's one of New England's most impressive wood-boring insects. These substantial beetles can reach up to 2 inches in length, with a broad, flattened brown body that looks almost mahogany-colored in good light. They belong to the longhorn beetle family, known for their characteristically long antennae, though the Brown Prionid's antennae are more moderately sized compared to some of their flashier relatives. This is actually the only species in its genus, making it quite special among New England's beetle fauna.

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Large and hefty beetle, up to 2 inches long with a broad, robust body that feels surprisingly heavy if you pick one up - much more substantial than most beetles you'll encounter

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Rich reddish-brown to dark brown coloration, sometimes with a slight mahogany sheen that catches the light beautifully

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Moderately long antennae that are slightly serrated or saw-toothed, especially noticeable in males - run your finger gently along them to feel the subtle teeth

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly flattened appearance from above, with a wide thorax and parallel-sided wing covers that give it an almost rectangular outline

idTips.label: Jaws
idTips.description: Prominent, powerful-looking mandibles (jaws) that project forward noticeably - these are built for chewing through tough wood

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, almost polished-looking surface with a hard, armor-like feel when touched - quite different from fuzzy or bumpy beetles

habitat: Brown Prionids are found in mature hardwood and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly where there are large dying or recently dead trees like oak, maple, and birch. The larvae develop in rotting wood, so adults are often found near fallen logs, dying tree trunks, or areas where trees have been damaged by storms. They prefer established forests rather than young woodlands, as they need substantial dead wood for their lengthy larval development.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their woody nurseries in late spring, though they're not commonly seen yet. Look for exit holes in dead hardwood logs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are most likely to be spotted, often attracted to lights at night or found crawling on or near dead wood during warm evenings.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity continues into early fall, though numbers decline. This is when mating and egg-laying occurs in suitable dead wood.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off, but larvae are actively feeding inside dead logs and stumps, slowly growing through their multi-year development cycle.

funFact: Brown Prionid larvae can take up to 7 years to complete their development, spending all that time as wood-eating grubs inside a single rotting log - imagine the same bug chewing away in there from kindergarten through middle school!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other large, brown longhorn beetles, but the Brown Prionid's hefty, flattened build and substantial size usually set it apart. Remember: if it's really big, really brown, and really robust-looking, you've probably found New England's only prionid. The prominent jaws are also a good distinguishing feature.
contextualKnowledge: The Brown Prionid holds the distinction of being the sole representative of its genus Orthosoma, making every individual you encounter part of an exclusive club. Interestingly, scientists once used the name Orthosoma for a completely different type of organism (a microscopic parasite), but had to change that name since the beetle got there first in scientific naming.
compareHints: Since the Brown Prionid is the only species in its genus, it's best compared to other large longhorn beetles in New England. Unlike the more colorful or patterned longhorns, the Brown Prionid is uniformly brown and much more robust and flattened. It's significantly larger and heavier-built than most other longhorn beetles you'll encounter, with a more rectangular, armor-plated appearance rather than the sleeker look of its relatives.
